title: Twin Primes in Special Forms
description: Twin prime pairs (p, p+2) where both are prime must have the form (6k-1, 6k+1) for p > 3. A structural theorem constraining where twin primes can occur.

overview.historicalContext:
Twin primes have fascinated mathematicians since antiquity. The ancient Greeks knew about pairs like (3,5), (5,7), (11,13), and the pattern seems to continue indefinitely, though primes become increasingly sparse.

The Twin Prime Conjecture—that there are infinitely many twin prime pairs—remains one of the most famous open problems in mathematics. While Zhang Yitang's 2013 breakthrough showed there are infinitely many primes differing by at most 70 million (later reduced to 246 by the Polymath project), the gap of exactly 2 remains elusive.

This formalization proves a structural result: twin primes greater than 3 must have a specific form, constraining where to search for them.
overview.problemStatement:
**Definition**: A pair (p, p+2) is a **twin prime pair** if both p and p+2 are prime.

**Examples**: (3,5), (5,7), (11,13), (17,19), (29,31), (41,43), ...

**Structure Theorem**: For p > 3, if (p, p+2) are both prime, then p ≡ 5 (mod 6).

Equivalently, twin prime pairs greater than (3,5) have the form (6k-1, 6k+1).
overview.text: Twin prime pairs (p, p+2) where both are prime must have the form (6k-1, 6k+1) for p > 3. A structural theorem constraining where twin primes can occur.
overview.proofStrategy:
The proof uses modular arithmetic modulo 6:

1. **All primes > 3 are ≡ 1 or 5 (mod 6)**: Primes > 3 cannot be divisible by 2 or 3.

2. **If p ≡ 1 (mod 6)**: Then p + 2 ≡ 3 (mod 6), meaning 3 divides p + 2. Since p > 3 implies p + 2 > 5 > 3, we have p + 2 composite—contradiction.

3. **Therefore p ≡ 5 (mod 6)**: The only remaining possibility.

This means twin primes (p, p+2) with p > 3 straddle a multiple of 6: if p = 6k - 1, then p + 2 = 6k + 1.
keyInsights: The structure theorem eliminates half of potential starting points
Similar to Sophie Germain prime structure (also $p \equiv 5 \pmod{6}$) — not coincidental, as both require the companion number to avoid divisibility by 3
Both $p$ and $p+2$ must avoid being divisible by 2 or 3; since all primes $> 3$ are $\equiv \pm 1 \pmod{6}$, twin primes must straddle a multiple of 6

**Hardy-Littlewood conjecture**: The number of twin primes up to $N$ is asymptotically $2C_2 N/(\ln N)^2$ where $C_2 = \prod_{p \geq 3}(1 - 1/(p-1)^2) \approx 0.6602$ is the twin prime constant — this uses the same sieving ideas as the $6k \pm 1$ structure
prerequisites: Analytic number theory (prime gaps, sieve methods)
Elementary number theory (prime distribution, twin primes)

sections.title: Definitions
sections.summary: Formal definitions of twin prime pairs and the conjecture.
sections.mathContext: Formal definitions: a twin prime pair is $(p, p+2)$ where both $p$ and $p+2$ are prime. The twin prime conjecture: there are infinitely many twin prime pairs. The strongest known result is Zhang (2013) / Maynard-Tao (2014): $\liminf(p_{n+1} - p_n) \leq 246$.

sections.title: Structure Theorem
sections.summary: The main result: twin primes > 3 must satisfy p ≡ 5 (mod 6), giving form (6k-1, 6k+1).
sections.mathContext: The main structural result: for twin prime pairs $(p, p+2)$ with $p > 3$, we have $p \equiv 5 \pmod{6}$, so the pair has the form $(6k-1, 6k+1)$. Proof: among $6k, 6k+1, \ldots, 6k+5$, only $6k \pm 1$ can be prime (the others are divisible by 2 or 3), so twin primes must straddle a multiple of 6.

sections.title: The Conjecture
sections.summary: The twin prime conjecture stated as an axiom.
sections.mathContext: The twin prime conjecture: $\{p : p \text{ and } p+2 \text{ are both prime}\}$ is infinite. Stated as an axiom in Lean since it remains unproved. Related to the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture on the asymptotic density $\pi_2(x) \sim 2C_2 x/(\ln x)^2$ where $C_2 \approx 0.6602$ is the twin prime constant.

sections.title: Non-Examples
sections.summary: Why 0, 1, and 2 cannot start twin prime pairs.
sections.mathContext: Why 0, 1, and 2 cannot start twin prime pairs: 0 and 1 are not prime, and while 2 is prime, $2 + 2 = 4$ is not. The pair $(2, 3)$ has gap 1, not 2, so it is not a twin prime pair by definition.

crossReferences.description: Zhang/Maynard-Tao proved lim inf of prime gaps is finite; the twin prime conjecture asks if this limit is 2
The infinitude of primes is necessary context — the twin prime conjecture asks if infinitely many primes come in pairs
The PNT gives the density of primes; the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture predicts twin prime density using a similar asymptotic framework
Dirichlet's theorem guarantees primes in arithmetic progressions; the 6k±1 structure of twin primes reflects primes in residue classes mod 6
The divergence of $\sum 1/p$ shows primes are dense enough for the sum to diverge; Brun's theorem shows the analogous sum $\sum 1/p$ over twin primes converges, quantifying their relative sparsity
Bertrand's postulate guarantees a prime in $(n, 2n)$, ensuring prime gaps grow at most linearly — a weaker but unconditional result compared to the conjectured bounded gaps between twin primes
Sophie Germain primes $p$ where $2p+1$ is also prime share the $p \equiv 5 \pmod{6}$ constraint with twin primes — both require the companion number to avoid divisibility by 3
Wilson's theorem $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$ provides a primality characterization; for twin primes $(p, p+2)$, the pair of Wilson congruences constrains $p \bmod 6$

conclusion.summary:
This formalization proves a clean structural result about twin primes: those greater than 3 must have the form (6k-1, 6k+1). The proof elegantly uses modular arithmetic to show that p ≡ 1 (mod 6) leads to p+2 being divisible by 3.

Notably, this is the same residue class constraint as Sophie Germain primes—both require p ≡ 5 (mod 6) for p > 3. This isn't coincidental: in both cases, the 'companion' (2p+1 or p+2) would be divisible by 3 if p ≡ 1 (mod 6).
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: **Search Optimization**

The structure theorem means we only need to check numbers of the form 6k-1 when searching for twin primes greater than 3.

This immediately eliminates half of all candidates.

**Sieve Algorithms**

Twin prime sieves can use this to be more efficient: after sieving for primes, only check pairs straddling multiples of 6.

**Connection to Goldbach**

Every even number ≥ 8 can be written as 6k ± something. Understanding twin primes around multiples of 6 connects to additive problems.
